newsitem.title: USA: US panel mulls risk of stock market decline - paper.
newsitem.headline: US panel mulls risk of stock market decline - paper.

text.p: A financial policy panel advising President Bill Clinton last week discussed the risks of a stock market decline in the wake of recent gains in the Dow Jones industrial average, the Washington Post reported Sunday.

Officials attending Tuesday's meeting of the Working Group on Financial Markets, created after the 1987 stock drop, considered whether prices on the stock market reflected a greater appetite for risk-taking by investors, it said.
Some expressed concern that the higher the market went, the more likely it would trigger a correction, the newspaper quoted sources familiar with the meeting as saying.
The group meets regularly to discuss options and review crisis scenarios for another market drop.

Its members include Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt, Jr. and Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Brooksley Born.
Their main goal would be to limit the extent of a sudden downturn.

Officials said they were confident that the conditions that led to the slide a decade ago were not present today, the Post reported. They cited low interest rates and a healthy economy as key differences between now and 1987.
Officials also pointed to SEC-approved "circuit breakers" introduced after 1987 to give investors timeouts to calm down.
Rubin on Sunday repeated his forecast of solid U.S. economic growth with low inflation for the foreseeable future.
"I think the most likely outcome going forward is a continuation of solid growth and low inflation, Rubin said on the "Face the Nation" television program.
Rubin did not comment on the stock market's extended bull run, but the Post quoted its sources as saying he, Levitt and Greenspan were worried about the market's vulnerability.
